Middle English -al English -al English aerial From Latin āeri(us) + -al, from Ancient Greek ἀέριος (aérios), from ἀήρ (aḗr, “air”) + -ιος (-ios). By surface analysis, aer- (“air”) + -ial.

senses.d: Living or taking place in the air.
ex: The seabirds put on an astonishing aerial display.

senses.d: Made up of air or gas; gaseous.

ex: The aerial photographs clearly showed the damage caused by the storm.

senses.d: Pertaining to the air or atmosphere; atmospheric.
Pertaining to a vehicle which travels through the air; airborne; relating to or conducted by means of aircraft.
ex: an aerial view of the landscape

senses.d: A rod, wire, or other structure for receiving or transmitting radio, television signals etc.
A move, as in dancing or skateboarding, involving one or both feet leaving the ground.
A move that involves performing a full rotation while in the air, without touching any equipment such as a balance beam or panel mat with one's hands.
A highly-contrasting visual artifact in the form of a band or ring.
ex: Lanczos3 for sharp results. May produce aerials. — Krita 5.2.2
